flagged.title: 'Chemistry' — Graham Swift
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly claims Ralph is 'kind' and 'tries to include the grandfather' (F4), wrongly asserts that the grandfather's suicide by poisoning is never stated directly and only inferred (F3), and attributes the family's loss entirely to the grandmother while omitting the father's death (F2).

mark_affecting.quote: The emotional movement is actually driven by two major losses: First, is the back story: the grandmother's death before the story even opens... But then comes the disruption: the arrival of Ralph
His suicide by poisoning is never stated baldly to the reader. It's only confirmed through inference and the boy's partial understanding.
Ralph is actually kind, he tries to include the grandfather. He isn't some cartoon villain.

flagged.title: 'Odour of Chrysanthemums' — D.H. Lawrence
flagged.reason: The video repeats the incorrect claims from F8 that Elizabeth's daughter brings the sprig into the house and that the chrysanthemums represent the births of her children (illustrated with an invented illness on the slide), missing the crucial symbolic link to Walter being brought home drunk.

mark_affecting.quote: Second, her daughter actually brings a sprig inside the house, and this triggers Elizabeth's memories of life's massive key passages. Her wedding, the births of her children

flagged.title: 'My Polish Teacher's Tie' — Helen Dunmore
flagged.reason: The video completely inverts the climax and central character dynamics (F10 and F11), falsely claiming Stefan fails to recognize Carla due to class prejudice rather than recognizing her immediately and singing with her while the English staff mock him.

mark_affecting.quote: Then, a pen-pal scheme between British and Polish teachers pops up. Carla gets involved, and for weeks, the letters act as this total equalizer between her and a teacher named Steve, who also has Polish heritage
It's this agonizing humiliating climax where he looks right at her in the canteen and has literally no idea who she is.
he's trapped by his institutional assumptions. Because he's a teacher, he literally cannot fathom that his intellectual equal is standing right in front of him

flagged.title: 'Korea' — John McGahern
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly claims the father directly tells the son the story of Moran on the boat and describes the payment as life insurance, missing the crucial plot point that the emotional crisis occurs when the son overhears his father calculating the government death compensation with a friend.

mark_affecting.quote: And then, he casually tells him about Moran, a local guy. He explains how Moran's son emigrated to the USA... received a massive life insurance payout... He thinks about the timing of the story... realizes his dad might actually be hoping history repeats itself

flagged.title: 'A Family Supper' — Kazuo Ishiguro
flagged.reason: The video repeats multiple debunked claims, including stating that the father does not condemn Watanabe's murder-suicide (when he explicitly calls it a mistake), fabricating an overgrown garden symbol, and claiming the story ends before anyone rises from the table.

mark_affecting.quote: The father doesn't condemn his partner's violent end. In fact, Watanabe's act of murder-suicide is described with a kind of reverence, almost like an act of principle.
the mother dies accidentally after eating the fugu fish
Then we have the overgrown garden. Literally, sure, it's just untended plants. But on a deeper level, it symbolises the neglect, the loss, and the profound estrangement...
the story stops before we see whether anyone rises from the table

flagged.title: 'Invisible Mass of the Back Row' — Claudette Williams
flagged.reason: The video presents an entirely incorrect plot for the central incident (claiming the back row were falsely blamed for something they didn't do and suffered collective punishment) and omits the second half of the story set in England where the narrator is finally heard.

mark_affecting.quote: she roots the story deeply in the era of British colonial education in a Jamaican primary school

mark_affecting.video_says: Our narrator, a young girl sitting way at the back, is unjustly blamed for something she didn't do. Meanwhile, the favoured kid sitting safely at the front completely escapes justice. And the fallout? The narrator and her peers at the back face collective physical punishment.
mark_affecting.lesson_says: Hortense asks what Columbus was doing in the Caribbean anyway and is struck on the knuckles with a ruler for asking a question/thinking rather than being falsely blamed for something she didn't do.
